title: Short Stuff: Olestra
summary: Short Stuff episode on Olestra (polyester sucrose), the fat substitute developed by Procter & Gamble and approved by the FDA. The hosts cover the 1950s Seven Countries Study and the 1990s low-fat craze that led to demand for fat-free foods, Olestra's development (initially considered for infant formula), its side effects (abdominal cramping, loose stools, "pooping your pants"), the chemistry of why it passes through the body unmetabolized, its effect on vitamin absorption, the Wow!/WOW chip launch, the FDA warning label requirement and its removal in 2002, and its continued use under names like "light" or "fat free" products.

segments.title: Opening banter and Seven Countries Study
segments.summary: Hosts open with jokes about Olestra making people poop their pants, then blame the 1950s Seven Countries Study for fueling the fat-is-bad belief and the low-fat food trend.

segments.title: Low-fat craze and Olestra's origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1990s fat-free boom, including Healthy Choice sales, and say Procter & Gamble developed Olestra in the late 1960s, originally as a fat substitute, with testing that showed digestive side effects.

segments.title: FDA approval and warning label
segments.summary: Procter & Gamble pressed on despite the side effects. The FDA approved Olestra on condition that products carry a warning about abdominal cramping and loose stools. Olestra was marketed for Pringles and Frito-Lay chips.

segments.title: The chemistry of Olestra
segments.summary: Explanation that Olestra is a sucrose molecule surrounded by many hydrocarbon chains, too many for the body's enzymes to break down, so it passes through unmetabolized and mimics fat's taste and mouthfeel.

segments.title: Weight gain, vitamin loss, and WOW chip sales
segments.summary: The hosts say the body can get confused and still absorb natural fats, which may cause weight gain, and that Olestra can carry away vitamins and nutrients. They note early WOW chip sales and a study in which many participants got diarrhea after eating chips.

segments.title: 2002 label removal and continued use
segments.summary: The FDA dropped the warning label requirement in 2002. Olestra is still used in light or fat-free products like Lay's Light, Ruffles Light, and fat-free Ritz and Wheat Thins, without the Olestra name.

segments.title: Prunes tangent and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts joke about prune juice having no warning label and briefly discuss prunes as dehydrated plums, then close the episode with an email address.
